Begin with the two ends of 1940 to 1944 in southern England: the D-Day Story at Portsmouth, where the invasion sailed from, and the underground operations room at Uxbridge, from which Fighter Command's No. 11 Group fought the Battle of Britain.

Spend the day on London at war: the bunker beneath Whitehall from which Churchill directed the war, St Paul's as the symbol of the city surviving the Blitz, and the Imperial War Museum's account of the whole conflict.

Two places that helped Britain survive: Bentley Priory, Dowding's headquarters and the heart of the air defence system in 1940, and Bletchley Park, where the codebreakers read German Enigma and Lorenz traffic.

A day on two kinds of war against Britain: the bombed shell of Coventry Cathedral, destroyed in the raid of November 1940, and the Liverpool bunker from which the Battle of the Atlantic against the U-boats was run.
A full day at Duxford, a fighter station in the Battle of Britain and later home to American fighter groups, where hangars of aircraft trace the air war from the Spitfire to the bombers over Germany.
Into Kent, the front line of the Battle of Britain: Biggin Hill, the most famous fighter station of 1940 and heavily bombed, and Manston, the exposed coastal airfield closest to the enemy.

Finish in Britain at Dover, where the Dunkirk evacuation was directed from tunnels in the cliffs, and the national Battle of Britain memorial at Capel-le-Ferne, before the evening ferry across to Dunkirk.

Spend the day on Operation Dynamo, May to June 1940: the museum in the command bastion, the mole and beaches from which over 338,000 Allied troops were lifted, the fort on the perimeter and the wrecks still on the sands.

South from Dunkirk to the Wormhout massacre site, a reminder of the fighting retreat of 1940, then to the giant concrete sites built for the V-weapons at Éperlecques and La Coupole and the Atlantic Wall guns near Cap Gris-Nez.

A long drive south-west into Normandy, to the end of the campaign: the Falaise Pocket, where the German armies in Normandy were trapped and destroyed in August 1944, and Hill 112, scene of the bitter fighting west of Caen.

Caen was the British objective on D-Day and took two months to win; the Memorial sets out the whole war, and Pegasus Bridge marks where British glider troops opened the invasion just after midnight on 6 June.

Follow the British and Canadian invasion coast from the Merville Battery and Sword Beach at Ouistreham, past the Canadians at Juno, to Gold Beach and the remains of the Mulberry harbour at Arromanches.
A day on the bloodiest of the five beaches: the German guns at Longues-sur-Mer, the shore at Omaha where the American assault nearly failed, the American Cemetery above it and the Overlord Museum.

Begin in Bayeux, the first town liberated, with its museum and the largest British war cemetery in France, then head west past the German cemetery at La Cambe to the cliffs scaled by the US Rangers at Pointe du Hoc.

Finish in Normandy with the American western flank: Utah Beach, where the landing went comparatively smoothly, and Sainte-Mère-Église, the town taken by American paratroopers in the early hours of 6 June.

A long drive west into Brittany to Brest, the great naval port that became a German U-boat base and was besieged by the Americans in August and September 1944, leaving the city almost entirely destroyed.
Follow the Breton coast to the U-boat pens that the Allied bombers could not break: Keroman at Lorient, and Saint-Nazaire, whose great dock was put out of action by the commando raid of March 1942.

A long drive south-east to Oradour-sur-Glane, the village where an SS division murdered 643 people in June 1944, left in its ruined state as a memorial to the occupation and the reprisals against the Resistance.

After the drive north, a day on Paris under occupation: the museum of the Liberation and Jean Moulin, the memorial to the Jews deported from France, and Mont-Valérien, where more than a thousand hostages and résistants were shot.
Two surrenders, five years apart: the clearing at Compiègne where Hitler made France sign the armistice of June 1940, and the schoolhouse at Reims where Germany surrendered to Eisenhower in May 1945.
Follow the 1940 campaign east, from Sedan, where German panzers crossed the Meuse and broke the French front, to the Maginot Line fort at Schoenenbourg, which held out but was simply bypassed.
Natzweiler-Struthof in the Vosges mountains was the only concentration camp on French soil, holding Resistance prisoners from across Europe; afterwards the drive continues north into Luxembourg.

Begin the Battle of the Bulge on its southern flank in Luxembourg: the American cemetery at Hamm where Patton is buried, and the museum at Diekirch on the river Sauer, crossed by his Third Army in January 1945.

A day at the centre of the Bulge: Bastogne, the crossroads town held by the encircled 101st Airborne in December 1944, with its museum, memorial, McAuliffe's headquarters and the foxholes in the Bois Jacques.

Head north across the Bulge, from Houffalize and St Vith, where the German advance was delayed, to Baugnez, where American prisoners were massacred, and La Gleize, where Peiper's battle group was finally stopped.

A day where Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany meet: Fort Eben-Emael, taken by German glider troops in May 1940, and the two great American cemeteries at Henri-Chapelle and Margraten, before crossing to Aachen.

Into Germany for the autumn and winter of 1944–45: the Hürtgen Forest, a long and costly American battle, and Remagen, where the capture of the Ludendorff Bridge in March 1945 opened the way across the Rhine.

The southern part of Operation Market Garden and its aftermath: the tank battle at Overloon, the museum and Canadian cemetery at Groesbeek, and the memorial to the American paratroopers who crossed the Waal under fire at Nijmegen.
A day on the battle of Arnhem in September 1944, from the bridge held by Frost's battalion and the drop zones at Ginkel Heath to Oosterbeek, where the 1st Airborne Division made its last stand.
Begin with the German invasion of May 1940 at the Grebbeberg and the bombed centre of Rotterdam, then end with occupation and persecution at the Anne Frank House in Amsterdam.

A long drive east to two camps linked by the deportations: Westerbork, the Dutch transit camp from which Anne Frank and over 100,000 others were sent east, and Bergen-Belsen, where she died and which the British liberated in April 1945.
From Hamburg, where the firestorm raids of July 1943 killed some 35,000 people, drive east along the Baltic to Peenemünde, where the V-2 rocket was developed and tested.

Two camps north of Berlin: Ravensbrück, the largest concentration camp for women, and Sachsenhausen, a model camp for the SS system that held political prisoners, Soviet prisoners of war and many others.

A day in Berlin's government quarter, where the Nazi state was run and fell: the Reichstag, the Topography of Terror, the Holocaust memorial, the Führerbunker site, the Bendlerblock of the 20 July plot and the Soviet memorial.

From the villa at Wannsee where the 'Final Solution' was coordinated to Cecilienhof, where the victors decided post-war Germany, then the Soviet memorial at Treptow and Karlshorst, where Germany's final surrender was signed.
The Seelow Heights, where the Red Army broke the last German line before Berlin in April 1945, then a long drive east across Poland to Gdańsk.
A day in the city where the war began on 1 September 1939: Westerplatte, where the Polish garrison held out for a week, the defended Polish Post Office, and the Museum of the Second World War.

East from Gdańsk to Stutthof, the first camp set up outside Germany's borders, then across former East Prussia to the Wolf's Lair, Hitler's headquarters for the war against the Soviet Union and site of the 1944 bomb plot.
Drive south to Warsaw for a day on the Warsaw Rising of August to October 1944, the Home Army's 63-day battle for the city, told at the museum in the old tram power station.
Morning on the Warsaw Ghetto, its uprising of April 1943 and the Umschlagplatz from which its people were deported, then out to Treblinka, the extermination camp where most of them were murdered.
Two places of Operation Reinhard and the camps of the Lublin district: Majdanek, on the edge of Lublin and still largely intact, and Sobibór, where prisoners rose up and escaped in October 1943.
Bełżec, the first of the Operation Reinhard extermination camps, then west to Kraków and Oskar Schindler's factory, which tells the story of the city under German occupation.
A full day at Auschwitz, the largest of the Nazi camps, where about 1.1 million people were murdered: the main camp at Auschwitz I and the extermination camp at Birkenau.

A long drive west to Prague for Operation Anthropoid, the 1942 assassination of Reinhard Heydrich by Czechoslovak parachutists: the bend in Libeň where he was ambushed and the church crypt where they made their last stand.

Two places marked by the occupation of Czechoslovakia: Lidice, destroyed in reprisal for Heydrich's killing, and Terezín, the ghetto and transit camp of Theresienstadt, before crossing into Germany to Dresden.
A day in Dresden: the rebuilt Frauenkirche and the bombing of February 1945, and the Military History Museum, which looks at the war and German military history without glorifying it.
Two stories from Saxony: Colditz Castle, the camp for Allied officers who kept trying to escape, and Torgau on the Elbe, where American and Soviet troops met in April 1945.

Buchenwald, on the Ettersberg hill above Weimar, was one of the largest concentration camps inside Germany and was liberated by the Americans in April 1945; afterwards, a longer drive south to Nuremberg.

Nuremberg, the city of the Nazi Party rallies and of the war crimes trials: the vast unfinished rally grounds and their documentation centre, and Courtroom 600, where the leading Nazis were tried in 1945–46.

Dachau, the first concentration camp and the model for those that followed, then Munich, the birthplace of the Nazi movement, where the NS-Documentation Centre stands on the site of the party headquarters.

Above Berchtesgaden, the Obersalzberg was Hitler's mountain retreat and a second seat of government; the documentation centre explains it, and the Eagle's Nest stands on the summit above, before the drive on to Linz.

Mauthausen, near Linz, was the main camp of the Nazi system in Austria, where prisoners were worked to death in the granite quarry; its subcamp at Gusen, nearby, held still more and was even deadlier.
A separate trip, flying to Rome: Monte Cassino, the abbey-crowned hill that blocked the road to Rome for four battles in early 1944, with the Polish, Commonwealth and German cemeteries around it.
The Anzio landings of January 1944, the beachhead museum and the American cemetery at Nettuno, then Rome under German occupation: the Ardeatine Caves massacre and the Gestapo prison at Via Tasso.

A separate trip, flying to Malta, the island fortress that was besieged and bombed from 1940 to 1942 while it struck at Axis convoys to North Africa: the war rooms beneath Valletta and the museums at Fort St Elmo and Birgu.
A separate trip, flying to Crete, scene of the German airborne invasion of May 1941: Hill 107 and the airfield at Maleme, the fighting for Galatas, and the Commonwealth cemetery at Souda Bay.

A separate trip, flying to Oslo for the Resistance Museum and the story of the German invasion and occupation of Norway, then a drive west to Rjukan and Vemork, target of the heavy-water sabotage raids of 1943.
A flight north from Oslo to Narvik, the iron-ore port where British and German destroyers fought in April 1940 and Allied troops recaptured the town before being withdrawn as France fell.

Begin the war in the east at the Brest Fortress, which held out against the German invasion of June 1941, and Khatyn, the memorial to the hundreds of Belarusian villages burned with their inhabitants.
Moscow, which the Germans came close to reaching in late 1941 before the Soviet counter-offensive pushed them back; the Victory Museum on Poklonnaya Hill tells the Soviet story of the whole war.
Leningrad was besieged for almost 900 days, and around a million civilians died; the Piskaryovskoye Cemetery holds hundreds of thousands of them, and the siege museum explains how the city survived.

Stalingrad, the battle that turned the war in the east: the Mamayev Kurgan hill fought over for months, the ruined mill and Pavlov's House from the street fighting, and the German and Soviet cemeteries at Rossoshka.
Kursk, the great battle of July 1943 and the last major German offensive in the east: the tank battlefield at Prokhorovka and the memorial complex at Kursk.
